data.Sub Topic: Participants learn to think and design at the platform level rather than the pipeline level. The session walks through the major data-platform architecture patterns used today -- batch warehousing, streaming/event-driven pipelines, the lakehouse pattern and data mesh -- comparing their strengths, trade-offs and best-fit scenarios with real examples. Participants then practice selecting and justifying the right pattern combination for a real business scenario, instead of defaulting to whichever pattern they already know best.

data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to turn business expectations -- such as 'customer data must be queryable within seconds of an interaction' or 'transaction records must never be lost' -- into specific, measurable targets for throughput, freshness, consistency and durability. The session then shows how to encode these targets as automated checks, called fitness functions, that run continuously and flag the platform the moment it drifts from what was promised, rather than the problem being discovered only after a report goes wrong.
data.Hands-on Activity: Using the context diagram from the previous session, define data NFRs for the Transaction data source (freshness, throughput, durability targets) and draft one executable fitness function to guard the highest-priority NFR in the data pipeline.
data.Learning Outcomes: Data NFR specification and fitness-function sketch appended to the Meridian Financial Group architecture package.

data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to document and communicate the reasoning behind a data architecture decision using an industry-standard format called an Architecture Decision Record (ADR), so anyone joining the project later can understand why a choice was made without having to ask around. The session also covers how to run a structured peer design review -- similar to a code review, but for architecture -- so decisions are challenged and validated by others before they are locked in, rather than approved informally.
data.Hands-on Activity: Formalize the pattern decision from Session 1 as an Architecture Decision Record, then run a structured peer review of the data NFRs defined in Session 2 and log the review outcomes.

topic: Capacity Planning, Performance Diagnosis & Pipeline Resilience

data.Topic: Capacity Planning, Performance Diagnosis & Pipeline Resilience
data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to estimate, before a pipeline goes live, whether it will hold up under real-world data volume -- for example, how many transaction events it can ingest per second before it falls behind -- and how to spot likely bottlenecks such as a slow join, an undersized cluster or a skewed partition. The session then introduces Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), a structured way of asking 'what could go wrong here, and how bad would it be?' for every stage of the pipeline. Participants use the answers to design resilience patterns -- such as replay queues, dead-letter handling and checkpointing -- so that when something does fail, the pipeline recovers cleanly instead of silently losing or duplicating data.
data.Hands-on Activity: Build a capacity model and performance budget for the Transaction data pipeline using the NFRs from Session 2, then run a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis against the same pipeline and design resilience patterns for the top failure modes identified.

topic: Well-Architected Review & Multi-Service Cloud Data Platform Design

data.Topic: Well-Architected Review & Multi-Service Cloud Data Platform Design
data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to run a Well-Architected review -- a structured checklist, used across all major cloud providers, that examines a design for cost efficiency, security, reliability and performance before it is built. Using the outcome of that review, participants then design how the data platform will actually be laid out across multiple cloud services -- ingestion, storage, warehouse/lakehouse compute and orchestration -- working together, rather than treating cloud deployment as a single black box.
data.Hands-on Activity: Run a Well-Architected review against the Meridian Financial Group design produced in Modules 1-2, then design the multi-service cloud topology -- ingestion, storage and compute -- that will host the platform, including the AI-integrated feature.
data.Learning Outcomes: Well-Architected trade-off analysis and multi-service cloud architecture diagram for Meridian Financial Group.

topic: Infrastructure as Code for Data Platforms

data.Topic: Infrastructure as Code for Data Platforms
data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to turn a cloud data-platform architecture diagram into Infrastructure as Code (IaC) -- reusable, version-controlled scripts that create the pipelines, storage and warehouse environment automatically and consistently every time, instead of engineers manually clicking through a cloud console. This makes environments repeatable, auditable and far faster to stand up or tear down.
data.Hands-on Activity: Translate the cloud architecture diagram from the previous session into a golden-path Infrastructure-as-Code template for the Meridian Financial Group platform.

topic: Multi-Region Resilience & Release Strategy for Data Platforms

data.Topic: Multi-Region Resilience & Release Strategy for Data Platforms

topic: Zero Trust & Identity-Centric Design for Data Access

data.Topic: Zero Trust & Identity-Centric Design for Data Access
data.Sub Topic: Participants learn Zero Trust: the principle that no request should be trusted by default, even if it comes from inside the company network, and every access request to a dataset must be verified based on identity. The session teaches participants how to redesign an existing data platform's access boundaries around this principle -- including row- and column-level access control -- moving away from the older idea of a single secure 'perimeter' wrapped around the whole platform.
data.Hands-on Activity: Redesign the Meridian Financial Group platform's access boundaries using zero-trust principles, building directly on the threat model from the previous session.
data.Learning Outcomes: Zero-trust design for the Meridian Financial Group platform.

data.Sub Topic: Participants learn to think and design at the system level rather than the feature level. data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to turn business expectations -- such as 'the system must handle peak sale-day traffic' or 'orders must never be lost' -- into specific, measurable targets for scalability, availability and response time. topic: Performance Engineering, Failure Mode Analysis & Resilience

data.Topic: Performance Engineering, Failure Mode Analysis & Resilience
data.Sub Topic: Participants learn how to estimate, before a system goes live, whether it will hold up under real-world load -- for example, how many concurrent orders it can process before it slows down -- and how to spot likely bottlenecks such as a slow database query or an overloaded service. The session then introduces Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), a structured way of asking 'what could go wrong here, and how bad would it be?' for every part of the system. Participants use the answers to design resilience patterns -- such as retries, circuit breakers and fallback responses -- so that when something does fail, the system degrades gracefully (a slower or reduced experience) instead of crashing outright.
data.Hands-on Activity: Build a capacity model and performance budget for the Order service using the NFRs from Session 2, then run a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis against the same service and design resilience patterns for the top failure modes identified.
data.Learning Outcomes: Capacity model, FMEA worksheet and resilience pattern map, all scoped to the Order service.

data.Session Title: Program Kickoff & Banking Domain Immersion  🎯 Discipline Day 1
data.Hands-On / Workshop: Joint workshop: Engineering + MBA learners mixed into pods. Given a Straive banking brief, pods write a problem statement, hypotheses and KPIs together. Individual Scorecard issued and the Day 0 pre-assessment gap analysis reviewed 1:1 with each learner.
data.Assessment / Assignment: Individual: 1-page problem statement + hypothesis tree for an unseen banking case. Scored on clarity, business logic, actionability. Daily tracking begins today — attendance, SPL, submission and participation post to the Individual Scorecard every evening.
data.Banking Domain Use Case: Banking customer churn — problem framing exercise
data.AI Integration Touchpoint: Use Claude to critique your problem framing — compare AI suggestions against peer feedback and identify what each one misses. Gemini used for background research on the banking brief.
data.Core Topics — Live Session: Straive context: banking & payments business model, client landscape · consulting vs engineering problem-solving mindsets · SMART KPIs · hypothesis-driven thinking · common-then-split architecture · HOW YOU ARE MEASURED: Individual Scorecard, daily tracking and the 360° evaluation framework walked through on Day 1 so every learner knows the bar from the outset
data.Discipline Thread (Spec-First / Test-Fir: "Acceptance Criteria Before Approach" introduced BY NAME as the programme's operating principle. Every pod must write what a correct answer looks like before they are allowed to start solving — spec-first in plain language, before any tool is taught.
data.SPL — Self-Paced Topic (not counted in h: Banking & Payments 101 — industry primer, glossary, Straive org context

data.Session Title: Consulting & Engineering Mindsets + Repository Literacy
data.Hands-On / Workshop: Cross-functional pod exercise: MBA learners frame the business spec, Engineering learners frame the technical spec for the same banking problem, then trade and critique across discipline lines. Pods map their problem onto the data lifecycle and name who owns each stage. REPOSITORY SET-UP (45 min): every learner activates their GitLab account, clones the programme repository, commits the Day 1 problem statement and Day 2 spec with a written commit message, and confirms the commit appears in the history. Both tracks — the MBA cohort commits documents exactly as Engineering commits code.
data.Assessment / Assignment: Pod submission: paired business + technical spec for one banking scenario, peer-reviewed against a rubric. GATE: the spec must be committed to the learner's repository with a meaningful commit message — a first, low-stakes rehearsal of the repository discipline that becomes mandatory on Day 14.
data.Banking Domain Use Case: Digital onboarding friction — joint spec exercise
data.AI Integration Touchpoint: Compare a Claude-generated problem frame against the pod's own — identify the gaps the AI missed. Gemini used for market and competitor context.
data.Core Topics — Live Session: Decomposing ambiguous briefs · MECE structuring for technical and business contexts · spec-first thinking — why both disciplines benefit from writing the spec before building · THE DATA LIFECYCLE as the shared mental map for the next 15 days: source system → model → warehouse → pipeline → insight → decision · REPOSITORY LITERACY (light touch, 45 min, NEW): why version control exists and what problem it solves · repository, commit, branch and merge request explained in plain language for both tracks · why every piece of work in this programme is versioned and reviewed rather than emailed · what "main is protected" means and why. This is orientation only — the full Git & GitLab session, with branching strategies, merge conflicts, repository management and change management, is Day 14.
data.Discipline Thread (Spec-First / Test-Fir: Reinforces Day 1: pods peer-review each other's "acceptance criteria" from the prior day before starting today's spec exercise. From today the commit message carries the same discipline in miniature — every commit must say what changed and why, which is the habit the Day 14 merge-request description formalises.
data.SPL — Self-Paced Topic (not counted in h: Intro to Spec-First Thinking — short primer for non-engineers · Version Control in 20 Minutes — repository literacy primer

data.Session Title: SQL Foundations — Querying for Decisions
data.Hands-On / Workshop: Write 15 progressively complex queries on a banking transactions dataset · build a customer summary report using CTEs and window functions.
data.Assessment / Assignment: 10 business questions on the banking DB schema — write SQL for each. Scored on correctness, efficiency, readability AND whether the pre-written assertion matched the actual output.
data.Banking Domain Use Case: Payment transaction reporting — SQL portfolio
data.AI Integration Touchpoint: Use Claude to write a complex query, then evaluate it for efficiency problems, incorrect logic and missing edge cases.
